newsitem.title: USA: Key Democrat aide sees no U.S. power bill in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Key Democrat aide sees no U.S. power bill in 1997.

text.p: A key Democrat aide predicted Monday the U.S. House was unlikely to pass legislation this year to make all states open their power markets to competition.

"I would be stunned if we got it out of the House," said Susan Sheridan, counsel to the Democrats on the House Commerce Committee. But she said she would not be surprised if legislation was passed by the committee this year.
Republicans on the Commerce Committee are leading efforts to require states to give all consumers freedom to choose their power supplier by the end of 2000.
Commerce Committee chairman Thomas Bliley, R-Va., recently said he hoped the House would pass a bill by the end of this year.

Sheridan said legislation would be difficult to pass this year because there was no consensus yet either among consumers or states that Washington should step in to make all states open their electricity markets.

"States are not asking us to pre-empt them. They are not asking us to assist them," she said at an American Public Power Association conference, adding that states that wanted to break utility monopolies were already doing so.
Sheridan said lawmakers are being bombarded on all sides, and are not willing to rush into forcing customer choice on all states. "There is a level of skepticism," she said.

Public power groups, utilities owned by local governments which are able to sell electricity more cheaply than investor-owned utilities partly because of tax advantages, are concerned that deregulation could make them less competitive.

But House Republican legislation so far does not address public power, even though it serves one in seven Americans, because Commerce Committee Republican leaders say taxing of municipal utility bonds is outside their bailiwick.
But Sheridan said the committee's top Democrat, Rep. John Dingell of Michigan, believed public power should be discussed.
"Dingell says it's relevant. Before we start playing around with one piece of the system, we should see how it will affect other pieces," she said.
Before holding any hearings in committee on a bill, the Republicans plan to hold public meetings in six areas around the country, starting in April.
